# C09 dossier: hold-forever Handwerk platform (idea P004 "Meisterwerk", name already taken)

Research date 2026-10-18. About 38 searches and fetches. FX: 1 EUR = 1.15 USD. "Read" means I opened the page or PDF. "Snippet" means I saw it only in a search-result summary, so treat it as weaker. [M] means from memory, not verified. "My arithmetic" marks a number I computed from sourced inputs plus a stated assumption.

## Verdict up front

The revenue path is real and proven, but the business is not differentiated. Four funded platforms already show that buying German Handwerk firms can reach EUR 180M-2B of revenue. The "hold forever, Meister equity ladder" angle is already being advertised by at least four other buyers. The unproven core, that half of a target's revenue is recurring statutory inspection and service work, has no source anywhere I looked. Reaching $100M of bought revenue yields only about EUR 4-8M of operating profit before financing (my arithmetic). Judgment: wounded, about 4.5/10. It survives as a capital-allocation business that needs a sponsor. It does not survive as a startup. The gate's "strong" is too generous.

## 1. Competitors: gate list confirmed, and more found

**Confirmed (read unless marked):**
- **Konzmann** (21 firms, about 1,100 staff, about EUR 180M "total operating performance" in 2024, so not necessarily revenue). Adiuva Capital held it from 2016. KLAR Partners closed the purchase on 30 Oct 2025. https://kpmg-law.de/en/kpmg-law-and-tax-advise-adiuva-capital-gmbh-with-fact-books-on-the-sale-of-konzmann-group/ (snippet). In Mar 2026 it bought Herber & Petzel, a 55-person firm in Muenster: https://www.unternehmeredition.de/?p=86132. 21 firms in about 9 years is roughly 2 deals a year (my arithmetic).
- **HWP Handwerkspartner.** Adiuva held it 2019-2023, then sold to GRIP (Goldbeck family and Robens). About 1,250 staff. Its Oct 2024 add-on was a 20-person electrical firm. https://www.dcadvisory.com/news-deals-insights/deal-announcements/dc-advisory-acted-as-exclusive-financial-advisor-to-adiuva-capital-on-the-sale-of-hwp-handwerkspartner-to-goldbeck-robens-industrial-partners/ and https://kpmg-law.de/en/kpmg-law-advises-the-hwp-handwerkspartner-group-on-the-acquisition-of-manfred-teckenburg-elektroanlagen/ (snippets).
- **Builtech Group:** 51 firms, 2,000+ staff, calls itself a "reliable succession partner". Its owner is AUCTUS. VDK Groep (about 107 entities, EUR 1B+ revenue in 2024) agreed to buy it on 27 Nov 2025, giving about EUR 2B, 7,000+ staff and 150+ businesses. EU clearance was pending at announcement and I found no closing notice. https://webdisclosure.com/press-release/builtech-holding-gmbh-etr-europes-new-champion-in-the-skilled-trades-is-emerging-builtech-group-becomes-part-of-dutch-vdk-groep-ScUqQSpoNQo (read). VDK is itself a PE portfolio company of EMK Capital: https://emkcapital.com/news/emk-acquires-majority-stake-in-vdk-groep (snippet). Builtech bought Elstek (Leverkusen, 60 staff, founders stay) on 1 Apr 2026: https://www.unternehmeredition.de/builtech-group-erwirbt-leverkusener-spezialisten-elstek/ (read).
- PE targets "about 20 staff and EUR 2M revenue and up" (Ludwig-Froehler-Institut). The same study says the former owner usually stays 2-3 years. https://www.handwerksblatt.de/betriebsfuehrung/chancen-und-herausforderungen-durch-private-equity-investitionen-in-das-deutsche-handwerk (read).

**New competitors the gate did not list:**
- **Fire protection:** Waterland's Wtech Fire Group bought Feuerfuchs Brandschutz (29 Apr 2026, its first German add-on): https://www.hoganlovells.com/en/news/hogan-lovells-beraet-wtech-fire-group-limited-zum-zeitpunkt-des-vollzugs-eine-portfoliogesellschaft-des-private-equity-fonds-waterland-beim-erwerb-der-feuerfuchs-brandschutz-gmbh (snippet). svt/Ergon's fire group has 1,500+ staff and EUR 300M+: https://majunke.com/noerr-beraet-svt-unternehmensgruppe-und-ergon-capital-bei-dem-erwerb-der-technical-fire-safety-group (snippet).
- **Electrical:** Parcom bought a majority of EAB Elektroanlagenbau (snippet). Elevion's Elektro Decker (about 300 staff, NRW) bought H+R Elektromontagen: https://www.produktion.de/instandhaltung/elektro-decker-kauft-hr-elektromontagen/1742077 (snippet).
- **Hold-forever positioning is already taken.** S&V Mittelstandspartner (Munich, 19 investors) advertises "Kein Portfolio, kein Exit-Zeitplan, keine Zerschlagung" (30 Jul 2026), though it targets EUR 2-8M EBITDA, too big for this idea: https://www.etl.de/leistungen/match-unternehmensboerse/inserate/87989/ (read). An unnamed German buyer is seeking TGA firms with revenue from EUR 3M, 10+ staff, "langfristige Investition" (23 Jun 2026): https://www.etl.de/leistungen/match-unternehmensboerse/inserate/86326/ (read). EIBE Beteiligungen (Austria, founded 20 Jul 2026) rules out quick resale for electrical firms (snippet from a LinkedIn post). Purpose Evergreen Capital writes EUR 0.5-5M non-voting evergreen tickets for 8-13 years: https://purpose-economy.org/en/?p=194 (snippet). The gate also found about 15 German search funds. Typical search capital is EUR 300-600k: https://www.unternehmeredition.de/search-funds-die-neuen-wettbewerber-von-private-equity/ (snippet).
- **Free substitutes:** Handwerkskammer Nachfolgemoderatoren, nexxt-change, Betriebsboersen, and the owner simply closing. About 54,000 Handwerk firms plan closure against 49,000 planning a handover over two years: https://www.deutsche-handwerks-zeitung.de/?p=374071 (read).

**Point on "hold forever":** the PE platforms hold for about 4-9 years (Adiuva: HWP 2019-2023, Konzmann 2016-2025), so a genuine permanent holder is a real contrast. But owners can already buy that promise from S&V, an ETL client, or Mition-type succession funds. It is a pitch line, not a moat.

## 2. Bottom-up market

This is a buying business, so the "pool" is sellers and what they cost, not payers.

- **Universe:** 569,898 Handwerk firms in the 2022 census. 80.2% have fewer than 10 people and 59.8% fewer than 5. https://www.zdh.de/ueber-uns/fachbereich-wirtschaft-energie-umwelt/statistik/handwerkszaehlung/handwerkszaehlung-2022/ (read).
- **Target trades (snippet):** about 63,900 electrical firms (end 2023, assignment unconfirmed) and 50,500 plumbing and heating firms, from ZDH series https://www.zdh.de/daten-fakten/betriebszahlen/handwerk-im-zeitverlauf/. The average electrical firm has about EUR 1.8M revenue (ZVEH, via https://elektro.net/file/show/159673/091e8f/DE_2024_12_55_BF31_R.pdf).
- **Funnel (my arithmetic):** 114,000 firms x about 20% with 10+ people (derived from the 80.2% figure) = about 23,000. x 33% planning a handover within 5 years (HWK Dortmund: https://www.hwk-do.de/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Sonderumfrage-Betriebsnachfolge-im-Handwerk-Fruehjahr-2026.pdf) = about 7,500, or about 1,500 a year. Twelve deals a year is under 1% of that. Share is not the constraint. Execution is.
- **Warning:** two-thirds of all handovers involve firms with up to 9 employees. https://bw.ermoeglicher.de/documents/2237/PM_Nachfolgemonitor_VDB.pdf (read). The firms that PE ignores are mostly too small to carry a Betriebsleiter and a share of holding costs. The gate's "sub-EUR 2M firms are open" is true but mostly because they are unattractive.
- **Seller-side shock:** Handwerk insolvencies hit 4,950 in 2025 (rate 7.3 per 1,000, highest in over a decade). https://www.zdh.de/daten-und-fakten/kennzahlen-des-handwerks/insolvenzen-und-insolvenzquoten-im-handwerk/ (read). Only 50.5% see a family solution as feasible. https://www.unternehmeredition.de/familieninterne-nachfolge-im-handwerk-wird-zum-auslaufmodell/ (read). Supply of sellers is ample.
- **Path to $100M:** 60 firms x EUR 1.5M = EUR 90M ($103.5M). Arithmetic holds. All of it is acquired, none is built.

## 3. Evidence of demand and willingness to pay

Statutory duties are real, and they are the best part of the thesis:
- Passenger lifts need a ZUeS main inspection at least every 2 years plus an interim inspection, and the operator cannot extend the interval. https://www.tuvsud.com/de-de/indust-re/betriebssicherheitsverordnung-info/betriebssicherheitsverordnung-aufzug (snippet).
- DGUV V3 requires periodic electrical testing. Intervals for fixed installations are only a 4-year guide value and for mobile equipment are risk-based. https://forum-verlag.com/fachwissen/elektrosicherheit-und-elektrotechnik/prueffristen-nach-dguv-v3/ (snippet).
- Fire alarm systems need annual maintenance by certified staff, with detector replacement every 5 or 8 years. https://www.baunetzwissen.de/brandschutz/fachwissen/brandmeldeanlagen/wartung-und-instandhaltung-von-bma-3183031 (snippet).
- 21.5M heating systems exist, 4M older than 30 years (BDH, via https://vdiv.de/news-details/vier-millionen-heizungen-in-deutschland-sind-aelter-als-30-jahre, snippet). German technical-service providers grew 9.6% in 2025 inside a EUR 68.7B facility-services market. https://www.luenendonk.de/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/LUE_PI_FS_DE_Studie_2026_f-1.pdf (snippet).

**The missing proof:** I found no source on what share of a micro electrical or plumbing firm's revenue is recurring service. The only splits I found are new build plus renovation at roughly 31-33% of electrical revenue, and customers 39% private, 35% commercial, 13.5% public, 11.7% housing firms. https://www.deutsche-handwerks-zeitung.de/?p=368992 (snippet). Two undated SBZ articles on plumbing service contracts conflict (about 15-year versus about 4-year average duration). Private customers are low-value, churn-prone and price-sensitive. The gate's "at least 50% recurring statutory inspection" filter is a hope, not a datapoint. It plausibly holds for lift and fire service firms, and probably not for typical installers. Those service specialists are exactly where PE (svt, Waterland) is already buying.

**Contract-book retention:** the VDB monitor says about 65% of acquired firms reach or exceed prior revenue after handover, so about a third do not. (read, link above.)

## 4. Unit economics and analogs

- **Price:** FINANCE realised-deal corridor for Bau/Handwerk under EUR 20M revenue is 0.25-0.50x revenue. Electrical/digital industry is 0.75-1.15x. Mittelstand planners ask 1.2x on average and 0.6x at the median. https://www.kfw.de/PDF/Download-Center/Konzernthemen/Research/PDF-Dokumente-Fokus-Volkswirtschaft/Fokus-2026/Fokus-Nr.-526-Januar-2026-Nachfolge-Monitoring.pdf (read, page 6). Handwerk owners expect an average of EUR 453k, median EUR 375k, about 87% of revenue. https://www.deutsche-handwerks-zeitung.de/?p=374071 (read).
- **Margin:** I found no good Handwerk benchmark. The 2024 Busch-Jaeger operating comparison says electrical profitability "remains at a low level" (snippet, elektro.net link above). The idea's 6-9% operating margin is therefore unverified. Assumed in this section.
- **What the buyer earns (my arithmetic):** At 0.5x revenue and 7.5% EBIT, price is 6.7x EBIT. After about 2.5% of revenue in holding and back-office cost (my assumption), EBIT is 5% and price is 10x. After about 30% German tax (my assumption) that is a 7% unlevered yield on price. If sellers hold to 0.87x revenue, the yield falls to about 4%. Two gates matter: the price must stay under about 0.6x, and the 7.5% margin must be after paying a market-rate Betriebsleiter.
- **Contrast with the PE logic:** the buy-small, sell-big arbitrage (US home services: 2-3.5x seller earnings for micro firms, 5-8x EBITDA for $3-10M revenue firms, 9-13x for platforms, 17-20x exit claimed) is how Konzmann and HWP investors made money. https://beancount.io/blog/2026/07/11/hvac-plumbing-private-equity-roll-up-guide and https://digital.bnpmedia.com/article/OPINION/4994555/847866/article.html (snippets, blog-quality). A hold-forever buyer gives up that exit. Stanford search-fund data show 6.2-7.0x EBITDA entry and 33.9-35.1% IRR, but 26% of deals lose capital. https://www.papermark.com/blog/search-fund-guide (snippet). A permanent holder's return is yield plus modest growth, roughly 7-10% unlevered. That is LP-acceptable only for an insurer, Versorgungswerk or family office.

## 5. Capital needs

- Purchase consideration: EUR 36-54M at 0.4-0.6x of EUR 90M, or about EUR 78M at 0.87x (my arithmetic). Add working capital, a Betriebsleiter successor per firm, and holding overhead. The gate's EUR 15M seed covers about 2 years of deals at half-upfront.
- Debt is the soft spot. Buergschaftsbanken cap guarantees at EUR 2M per borrower since 2023 (period to end-2027). https://www.deutsche-handwerks-zeitung.de/?p=273451 (snippet). KfW 077 is a loan to natural persons within 5 years of starting self-employment, which a holding platform is not (gate's read of https://www.kfw.de/PDF/Download-Center/F%C3%B6rderprogramme-(Inlandsf%C3%B6rderung)/PDF-Dokumente/Produktinfos/6000005231_Produktinfo_077.pdf). Realistic plan: EUR 50-100M of sponsor equity plus bank debt on EUR 5M+ EBITDA, which is institutional capital. I found no hold-forever Handwerk fund to benchmark against.

## 6. Regulatory and liability landscape

- **Premise holds:** a GmbH or partnership is entered in the Handwerksrolle if its Betriebsleiter qualifies (Meister, engineer, certain others). https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/hwo/__7.html (read).
- **The bite:** an employed Betriebsleiter needs a real employment contract, normally full-time, genuine technical control, "appropriate" pay (collective-agreement benchmark), and leading several firms is allowed only in exceptions. https://www.hwk-do.de/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/Anerkennung-von-Betriebsleitern.pdf and https://www.hwk-ulm.de/wp-content/uploads/Merkblatt-Betriebsleiter.pdf (snippets). Sham arrangements are void (BAG, case number unverified). So every acquired A-trade firm needs its own qualified person once the old owner leaves after 2-3 years. Whether a tuck-in can run as a branch of a hub under one Betriebsleiter is unresolved. The chamber decides case by case. This is the binding constraint, and it is also the "Meister equity ladder" rationale.
- **Meister supply:** about 20,040 Meister exams passed across all Handwerk in 2019 (https://ice.dzhw.eu/portal/de/Tabelle-2.7.14.pdf, snippet). I found no 2024 figure for electrical or plumbing. 60 firms need 60 Meister over 5 years, which is small nationally but hard locally.
- **Deal structure [M]:** sole proprietors need asset deals. Asset deals move staff by section 613a BGB and need customer consent to assign contracts. Share deals keep history liabilities (warranty claims) inside the GmbH. Customer-list sale raises GDPR questions. None of this was verified this run.
- **Heating demand backdrop:** the Gebaeudemodernisierungsgesetz passed on 10 Jul 2026 and drops the 65% renewable rule. Heat-pump sales still rose 40% in H1 2026 (194,500 units) while subsidy per job falls EUR 750 every half-year. https://www.pv-magazine.de/2026/08/11/waermepumpen-sind-aktuell-wichtigster-wachstumstreiber-im-heizungsmarkt/ (snippet). Policy risk for plumbing and heating firms is live.

## 7. Is the "why now" real?

Partly used up and partly real.
- **Real:** Handwerk sellers outnumber buyers (54,000 planned closures, 49,000 handovers over two years), distress is at a decade high, and the VDB says Handwerk succession problems are especially acute.
- **Used up:** institutional buyers of 20-60-person firms are active in electrical, TGA and fire (Konzmann/KLAR, HWP/GRIP, Builtech/VDK, svt, Waterland, Parcom). The only gap is sub-EUR 2M firms, which is where price expectations and owner dependence are worst.
- **The 12 months matter:** Builtech/VDK and Konzmann/KLAR both changed hands in the past year. That means large pools of capital are now chasing Handwerk add-ons, which will raise prices for exactly the firms this platform wants.

## 8. Do the upside-case assumptions hold?

| Assumption | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Buy at 0.4-0.6x, half deferred | Plausible only for sellers with no alternative. Seller ask is 0.87x average and rising competition lifts it. Partly holds. |
| At least 50% recurring statutory revenue | Unverified. No source found. Likely true for lift and fire service, unlikely for installers. This is the make-or-break test. |
| 6-9% operating margin | Unverified. Profitability described as low. Insolvency rate 7.3 per 1,000 in 2025. |
| 12 deals a year | Konzmann did about 2 a year. Even PE-backed VDK averaged about 9 a year over 12 years (my arithmetic from 107 entities since 2013). A seed-funded entrant doing 12 a year with a Betriebsleiter for each is optimistic. |
| EUR 15M seed | Too small by a factor of 3-6. |
| Hold-forever as counter-positioning | Already advertised by others. Cheap to copy. |
| Meister equity ladder | Legally workable (employed Betriebsleiter). I found no precedent in Germany. Real design risk. |
| $100M revenue means a big business | Revenue is bought. About EUR 4-8M of operating profit at $100M of revenue (my arithmetic), before financing. |

## 9. Kill tests (cheapest first)

1. Get anonymised ledgers for 6-8 target firms and measure recurring share and 3-year customer retention. Stop if recurring revenue is under 40%.
2. Three non-binding term sheets at 0.6x or lower with half deferred. Stop if sellers insist on over 0.8x in cash.
3. Ask two Handwerkskammern in writing whether a tuck-in can be a branch under a hub Betriebsleiter. Stop if each acquired firm needs its own full-time Meister.
4. Five conversations with Versorgungswerk, insurer or family-office CIOs. Stop if none accepts a 7-10% unlevered yield with no exit.

## 10. Gaps

No source found for: recurring-revenue share by trade; operating margins of German micro Handwerk firms; actual traded multiples of sub-EUR 2M firms (only the FINANCE corridor); XPartners' German plans and the "Meisterwerk" trademark claim (not re-checked); Meister exam counts for electrical and plumbing; branch rules for Betriebsleiter; whether Builtech/VDK has closed.

## Scorecard (my judgment)

Size 6, defensibility 3, evidence of demand 5, capital-feasibility 4, why-now 4. Overall about 4.5/10. Better than the round-1 finalists on size, worse on moat. Not dead, not strong.

# C07 dossier: "Day 21" (P108, idea 7), multi-state operator of full-service forensic restoration beds

Date: 2026-10-18. About 55 searches and fetches, including the 117-page Ward v. Muth opinion, a live HHSC bed contract, and Colorado's April 2026 budget memo. Tags: [S] sourced, [D] my arithmetic on sourced inputs, [A] assumption or judgment. Where a page would not load and I used a search-result summary, I say so.

## 1. Bottom line

**Verdict: wounded, close to dead on the $100M test. Overall 4/10, upside 4/10.** This is the best-evidenced finalist in the pool. A federal injunction exists, a named agency owns the budget line, and a signed HHSC contract for a close variant of this product (16 geriatric forensic restoration beds) is public. But the idea fails lessons.md rule "big AND defensible" on four counts:

1. **The $100M path needs about 410 beds at the real Texas price, not 600 at $450.** That is roughly the size of the largest incumbent's entire Florida forensic footprint (446 beds, built since 2005-07). Realistic uncontested Texas demand is 150-400 beds, and Texas is already building or granting most of the rest.
2. **The order does not require Texas to buy anything.** HHSC says it is not ordered to fund a project or contract, the state is appealing, the waitlist has already fallen 40% from its peak, and HHSC did not ask for new bed funding in the 2026-27 session.
3. **The idea's price and speed assumptions are wrong in both directions.** $450 a day matches neither the jail-based product ($261-421) nor the hospital product ($697-1,050). "6-12 months, modular" collides with a hospital-licence-plus-Joint-Commission requirement.
4. **Incumbents are deep and the state is financing county-built shells that incumbents then manage.** Wellpath Recovery Solutions runs the Montgomery County model (county builds with a state grant, operator manages as "junior partner"). The thin moat the gate rated is thinner.

## 2. Assumption ledger (upside case tested)

| Claim in idea or gate | What I found | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Fifth Circuit risk is the main break point | Ezra denied a stay in August; Texas asked the Fifth Circuit to pause benchmark-setting; I found no ruling as of Oct 18 ([San Antonio Report](https://sanantonioreport.org/texas-court-order-competency-wait-21-days-bexar-county/), [Medical Daily](https://www.medicaldaily.com/texas-appeal-psychiatric-hospital-bed-competency-ruling-477301)). The gate's "2012 order paused" did not verify: the case was filed in 2016, and the Tribune says an earlier 2012 suit was lost ([Texas Tribune](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/08/11/texas-state-hospital-bed-mental-health-trial-competency/)). | Open, unquantifiable |
| HHSC "already buys 747 private beds" proves a forensic budget line | True number, wrong inference. Opinion footnote: "the vast majority of these purchased beds are civil." HHSC's behavioral-health arm holds only two inpatient restoration contracts (Harris Center 56 admitted, ACCESS 46 in FY25) ([opinion](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.txwd.830382/gov.uscourts.txwd.830382.266.0.pdf), [HHSC April 2026 deck](https://www.hhs.texas.gov/sites/default/files/documents/april-2026-jcafs-agenda-item-7.pdf)) | Overstated |
| Texas gap is "1,000+ beds" | HHSC's deputy commissioner testified that even with 434 new beds and about 416 added contracted beds by 2027 (some not full until 2028-29), HHSC stays 315 beds short of the 2024 CannonDesign need. The $270M "treat everyone on the waitlist in contract beds" figure is a one-time backlog ([opinion](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.txwd.830382/gov.uscourts.txwd.830382.266.0.pdf), ¶54, 118, 134) | Not supported |
| $450 per bed-day | HHSC's own contract with a private hospital implies about $697; Colorado pays $1,050 for contracted hospital beds and $421 for jail-based; a Texas state hospital bed costs $1,013 (section 4) | Wrong both ways |
| 6-12 months to deploy | Montgomery County's 100-bed addition: groundbreaking Aug 2025, patients Feb 2027, about 18 months, on an existing licensed campus ([Community Impact](https://communityimpact.com/conroe-montgomery/development/montgomery-county-mental-health-treatment-facility-breaks-ground-on-100-bed-expansion/)) | Refuted for hospital beds |
| Washington is a second market | State forecast: jail inpatient waits under 7 days after Olympic Heritage and Maple Lane; a 350-bed state hospital opens Aug 2028 ([WA legislature slide, search summary](https://app.leg.wa.gov/committeeschedules/Home/Document/262778)). The $100M Washington fine I found is dated 2023, not 2026 ([Colorado memo](https://content.leg.colorado.gov/sites/default/files/HUM%20BA8%20Memo%2004-22-26.pdf)). | Largely closed |
| "A bed pays for itself via fines" | Texas has no per-day fines in the injunction. Colorado's fines are capped at $12.8M in FY27; Oklahoma's were capped at $3.5M through March 2026 ([Colorado memo](https://content.leg.colorado.gov/sites/default/files/HUM%20BA8%20Memo%2004-22-26.pdf), [Public Radio Tulsa](https://www.publicradiotulsa.org/local-regional/2025-11-20/oklahoma-agency-fined-over-competency-restoration-settlement)) | Only partly true |
| Dallas County is a customer ("already suing the state") | Dallas lost: the 15th Court of Appeals held counties bear detention cost and the Texas Supreme Court declined review ([KERA, search summary](https://www.keranews.org/government/2024-08-23/texas-fifteenth-court-of-appeals-supreme-court-dallas-county-mentally-ill-inmates-health-and-human-services)). Cost was a little under $800k for 382 people in December, about $67 per person-day [D]. | Counties are not payers |

## 3. Bottom-up market

- **Texas stock and trend.** Waitlist 1,628 at end of June 2026; Sept-June monthly average 1,669, down 19% from 2,058 a year earlier ([San Antonio Report](https://sanantonioreport.org/texas-court-order-competency-wait-21-days-bexar-county/)). The peak was 2,711 in December 2022 ([State Auditor data](https://sao.texas.gov/Reports/DataSupplement/25-007Interactive.html)), so the list is down 40% [D]. HHSC reports 2,110 operational forensic beds against 2,299 funded; projects since 2017 add more than 680 state-owned beds; grants may add up to 332 more ([TPR](https://www.tpr.org/criminal-justice/2026-08-23/bexar-county-defendants-wait-months-in-jail-for-competency-treatment-judge-says-texas-is-violating-their-rights)).
- **Texas flow.** Demand grew 100-300 commitments a year recently, implying 1,000-4,000 more orders over four years than the last four ([opinion](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.txwd.830382/gov.uscourts.txwd.830382.266.0.pdf), fn. 29). My read: the recurring contractable gap is the 315-bed shortfall plus growth, perhaps 150-400 beds by 2030 [A].
- **National.** 32 of 40 reporting states have adult waitlists, but the mean is 137 people and the median 48 across 24 states; 14 of 39 states have been sued ([NRI, June 2026](https://nri-inc.org/media/df0dzlmu/nri-2024-2025-state-profiles-report-competency-restoration_june2026.pdf)). The big stocks are Texas (1,628), Georgia (697 jailed awaiting restoration, 187-day average) and Colorado. Georgia is building its own: $409M for a state hospital plus $20.7M for a 40-bed jail unit ([DBHDD](https://dbhdd.georgia.gov/press-release/2026-04-06/statement-agreement-between-dbhdd-and-gaoschr-regarding-forensic-0)). California spent $2B since 2021 and cut its list from 2,000 to under 300 ([Colorado memo](https://content.leg.colorado.gov/sites/default/files/HUM%20BA8%20Memo%2004-22-26.pdf)). Oklahoma's Forensic Center wait fell from 214 to 79 days between June and September 2025 ([Public Radio Tulsa](https://www.publicradiotulsa.org/local-regional/2025-11-20/oklahoma-agency-fined-over-competency-restoration-settlement)).
- **Colorado is the cleanest price-and-volume read.** Contract-bed spending rose from $3.4M (FY23) to $31.9M (FY27), +836%, while inpatient restoration orders rose 126% (750 to 1,696). Beds cut the list, then orders refilled it. The Special Master's report says neither jail-based nor contracted beds "should ever be the primary strategy"; Colorado's own staff recommended funding fewer contract beds than requested (16 of 27) ([memo](https://content.leg.colorado.gov/sites/default/files/HUM%20BA8%20Memo%2004-22-26.pdf)).
- **What $100M takes.** At 95% occupancy: about 640 beds at $450, 414 at $697, 275 at $1,050 [D]. A 414-bed operator is about the size of Wellpath's Florida forensic estate (238 + 208 = 446 beds, [TAC](https://www.tac.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Florida-State-Hospital-System-2023.pdf)). # C12 dossier: Outside Care Plan (P108, the DOC's own off-site health plan)

Prepared 2026-10-18. Tags: (S) read in a source this session, (A) my arithmetic or assumption, (U) secondary, aggregator or search-summary only. About 45 searches and fetches, including the Pew 2018 PDF, the DOJ OIG reports, Polk County's sole-source notice and Limestone County's Heritage contract.

## Bottom line

The pain is real. State prisons pay for off-site care at rates that auditors have called far above Medicare, and failed vendors left hospitals unpaid. But I found no state that has paid a third party to take hospital risk on a per-member-per-month basis, and none that I found tried it in 2026. Every 2026 buyer swapped one full-service vendor for another. The spending that does get unbundled goes to low-fee claims and network administrators. A risk-bearing version can reach $100M of revenue only as pass-through premium. At 5-8% margin that is $5-8M a year of profit, which needs 3-4 statewide wins in a market that procures a few contracts a year. Verdict: **weak, closer to kill than to advance.** My view of year 5-7 premium: $0 (about 55%), $25-40M (about 35%), $100M+ (about 10%) (A).

## 1. Competitors and substitutes (gate list checked, then extended)

**Confirmed, with new numbers**
- **Heritage Health Solutions** (Coppell, TX) is the closest incumbent, and the gate saw only its county work.
  - It has run the U.S. Marshals' nationwide managed-care contract since 2007, re-awarded 2017 and running to FY2027. From Oct 2017 to Sept 2024 the USMS spent about $398M on medical care and $222M on drugs through it, and paid Heritage about $40M in fees. It reprices every claim to the lowest of Medicare, the network rate or billed charges, under 18 U.S.C. 4006. [DOJ OIG 25-096](https://www.oversight.gov/sites/default/files/documents/reports/2025-09/25-096.pdf) (S)
  - County work: Polk County FL is sole-sourcing a five-year TPA contract in 2026. The notice requires a TPA license, URAC "Full" accreditation, and contracts with all five Polk hospitals, and it applies Medicare-based statutory repricing. [Polk ISS 26-293](https://www.polkfl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/ISS_26-293_Inmate_Medical-Pharmaceuitical_Services.pdf) (S)
  - Limestone County AL pays Heritage $40 per claim. Claims are invoiced at 140% of the Medicare allowable, and in-network providers are paid within 45 days. [Limestone minutes](https://limestonecounty-al.gov/files/assets/public/v/1/meetings-and-minutes/2024/07/7-15-24-cmm.pdf) (S) Coshocton OH planned $50 per claim. (U)
- **Prime Health Services** runs savings-share repricing through seven sheriff-association programs since 2011 and claims $88M+ of cumulative savings with no savings, no fee. [Prime](https://primehealthservices.com/markets/corrections/) (S for the claim, vendor-reported).
- **CorrectCare Integrated Health and NaphCare** (Safety Net Connect, which the gate listed, was not rechecked): NaphCare describes itself as managing off-site care for the BOP. [DOJ press release](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/prison-health-care-provider-naphcare-agrees-settle-false-claims-act-allegations) (U) CorrectCare is a corrections-only UM, network and claims shop, with revenue of about $7.6M from an unverified profile. [agentman](https://agentman.ai/medman/payers/correctcare-integrated-health-non-louisiana-jails) (U)

**Found that the gate missed**
- **Correctional Health Partners** (Denver) is a physician-owned TPA doing claims, prior authorization, network and pharmacy. It lists partnerships in CO, CA and OR and stopped delivering care in 2022. [Marit](https://www.marithealth.com/e/correctional-health-partners-oh3h3) (U) It bid Nebraska's DOC claims-payment RFP 120174 O3 against **BCBS of Nebraska, UMR (a UnitedHealthcare unit), Falling Colors and Innovative Claims Strategies**; intent to award was posted 4/29/25. [Nebraska DAS](https://das.nebraska.gov/materiel/purchasing/120174%20O3/RFP%20120174%20O3.html) (S) Even the plain claims function drew five bidders, including a UnitedHealthcare unit and the state Blue.
- **PGBA** pays North Carolina's inmate hospital claims. [NC DPS report](https://www.ncleg.gov/Files/Library/agency/dps12805.pdf) (S) California's network and prior-authorization contract was held by Health Net from 2014, and its current round (SD25-00019) uses a state-designated TPA for claims. [Govly](https://app.govly.com/public/opportunities/16772111) (U; sources give 8/18 and 10/30/2026 as the response date).
- **State self-administration is the biggest substitute.** Pew counts 17 states delivering care directly and 4 on a university model, and these pay hospitals from their own line. Five carve inpatient care out of vendor contracts (AR, IL, PA, VT, VA), 6 share risk and 8 use all-inclusive capitation. [Pew 2018](https://www.pew.org/-/media/assets/2018/07/prisons-and-hospital-care_report.pdf) (S, read from PDF text) The idea's "36 outsource, 14 in-house" does not match this.
- **Statute is the free substitute.**
  - Florida caps non-contracted providers at 110% of Medicare (125% if the provider has a negative margin). Enrolled county bills (HB 4059, 4041) and DOC bill HB 913 follow the same pattern. [FL House analysis](https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2026/913/Analyses/h0913c.JUB.PDF) (S)
  - New Hampshire's cap is 110% (S), North Carolina's default is twice Medicaid or 70% of charges (S), and Georgia law has a Medicaid-rate ceiling for non-contracted emergency care (U).
  - State Medicaid inpatient billing is a second substitute: North Carolina saved about $10M and Massachusetts about $5.8M a year. [Mass. auditor](https://www.mass.gov/news/audit-finds-58-million-in-annual-inmate-health-care-cost-savings) (S)

**Refuted or corrected:** the "Centene's Centurion" competitor. Two secondary sources say Centene sold Centurion in January 2023 to an undisclosed buyer; I could not find the primary filing. [AFSC](https://investigate.afsc.org/node/960) (U) No funded startup doing risk-based off-site care turned up. I searched Crunchbase-style sources and found only unrelated correctional firms (U).

**Moat read:** Payers (BCBS, UMR, PGBA) and Heritage already hold hospital contracts and TPA licenses, and statutes hand every competitor Medicare-based pricing for free. Only the risk transfer is new, and states have not bought it.

## 2. Bottom-up market

- **Pool:** Pew put state prison health spending at $8.1B in FY2015, which I grow to about $11B (A). Off-site is 20-27% of that: 20% across ten states, Virginia 27%, New York 23%. (S, Pew) That is $2.2-3.0B.
- **Reachable only where the DOC holds the risk.** Vendor-risk states are 8 of 40 classified (AZ, DE, FL, IN, KS, KY, MA, MO) and include big budgets. I take about 65% of spend as DOC-risk (A), then remove expansion-state inpatient stays that Medicaid already pays (Pew describes a "large shift"). That leaves **$1.1-1.8B** (A), close to the gate's $1.4-2.0B.
- **Per-state scale (S):**
  - Virginia: $62M off-site in FY2016, with nearly half spent on 179 people.
  - Oregon: $790K-$922K a week, or about $41-48M a year (A), and "nearly 25%" of its health budget. [Oregon LFO](https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2025I1/Downloads/CommitteeMeetingDocument/311156) (S)
  - North Carolina's UNC network alone: about $29-32M a year.
  - Texas hospital line: $137M of $435M in FY2012. [LBB](https://www.lbb.texas.gov/Documents/Publications/Info_Graphic/Correctional%20Managed%20Health%20Care%20Prepared%20for%20the%20Senate%20Finance%20Committee.pdf) (S, dated)
- **Revenue math:**
  - Risk-bearing: $100M of premium is roughly 5-9% of the pool. That is 2-3 mid-size states or one large one, at a 5-8% margin (gate and idea figure) or $5-8M of profit.
  - Fee model: Heritage's USMS take is about 10% of medical spend ($40M on $398M, A). Applied to the whole pool, the fee pool is about $110-180M, so 20% share is $20-35M. County claim fees at $40-50 are tiny: Polk's roughly 7,600 outpatient claims would be about $0.3M a year (A).
- **Federal and jails:** the BOP spent $327M on outside medical in FY2014 under per-institution contracts with third-party administrators. [DOJ OIG E-16-04](https://www.oversight.gov/sites/default/files/oig-reports/e1604.pdf) (S) The USMS is about $60M a year. Jails are bought county by county, and Wellpath's local-government contracts used "spending caps" on off-site care (U), so counties rarely hold uncapped risk to hand over.

## 3. Demand and willingness to pay

**For (real pain, weak proof of pay):**
- Oregon asked its legislature for $14.35M one-time because clearing an off-site backlog pushed weekly spend up 17% (790K to 922K). The DOC also bought new off-site billing services. (S)
- Unpaid hospital arrears from failed vendors: more than 750 Georgia providers claim $75.6M from Wellpath [JEMS](https://www.jems.com/ems-management/wellpath-bankruptcy-may-stick-ga-ems-with-state-prisoners-medical-bills/) (S); Michigan hospitals say they are owed $35M+ and EMS about $6M, under a risk-share contract. [Michigan AG letter](https://audgen.michigan.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/MDOC-Prisoner-Healthcare-Contract-Legislative-Request-–-AG-Letter-178293.pdf) (S)
- Overpayment audits: BOP institutions paid 115-385% of Medicare, and the OIG estimated at least $100M of excess in FY2014. North Carolina's audit found 467% and California's 250% of Medicare (U, PLN-style summaries).

**Against (what buyers actually did):**
- Alabama cancelled YesCare's roughly $1.06B contract and moved to an emergency NaphCare deal, 24 months, terms undisclosed. [ADOC](https://www.doc.alabama.gov/?p=534221) (S)
- Illinois ended Wexford's $4B deal for a one-year, $507M Centurion contract. [WBEZ](https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/07/07/illinois-department-of-corrections-health-care-contract-centurion-wexford) (S) Indiana extended Centurion by $213M and expected a new RFP, and Kansas moved to VitalCore at about $89M a year. [PLN](https://www.prisonlegalnews.org/news/2026/jun/1/kansas-doc-replaces-centurion-with-another-prison-healthcare-contractor/) (S)
- Florida went the other way from risk transfer: a cost-plus Centurion contract, with a markup cut from 13.5% to 11.5%, and a cost-reimbursed maximum of $572.6M rising to $584.8M. [Capitolist](https://thecapitolist.com/florida-department-of-corrections-locks-in-guaranteed-profit-for-vendor-despite-resistance-from-lawmakers/) (S)
- Texas's "capitated" university model leaves all deficits with the state, per the State Auditor. [SAO 25-012](https://sao.texas.gov/Reports/Main/25-012.pdf) (U) Governments keep the risk themselves.
- The closest live unbundling is California's SD25-00019: network plus prior authorization for about 90,000 people, five years plus five one-year options, and no risk transfer. It is a bellwether for the idea, not a win for it. (U)

**Who signs:** DOC commissioner or CFO, with legislative appropriation. No signer has been shown to hold a budget line for a risk transfer.

## 4. Unit economics

- **Fee analogs:** Heritage 10% of medical spend at federal scale; $40-50 per claim at county scale; Prime keeps a share of savings it documents itself.
- **Risk analog is bad.** Wellpath's court filings reportedly showed a combined negative gross profit of about $40M on its Michigan and Georgia contracts, 2022 to mid-2024. [Elevenflo](https://elevenflo.com/blog/wellpath-bankruptcy) (U; an aggregator summarizing filings). It also said it ended about 65 contracts for risk and insurance reasons. Michigan was a 50/50 risk share to a cap, and Georgia held hospital risk inside the vendor price. Wyoming's 50/50 off-site risk share lowered cost for the state, so risk sharing can help the buyer. [Wyoming LSO](https://wyoleg.gov/LSOResearch/2017/17RM011%20%20Binder%20Final%20(3)%207.21.2017.pdf) (U)
- **Pricing is adverse.** The DOCs with the worst off-site problems are the ones that most want to outsource, and their historical claims understate true demand (Oregon's 17% rise). Priced on the old run rate, a carve-out would have lost about $6.9M a year on a $41M base (A). Concentration is high (179 people drove nearly half of Virginia's $62M), so stop-loss matters. In a 2004 audit, hospital-contract stop-loss triggers cost California up to about $9.3M in one year. [Cal. auditor](https://information.auditor.ca.gov/reports/summary/2003-125) (S)
- **Price gap:** county contracts sit near Medicare plus 40%, while North Carolina's UNC deal is 240% of Medicare. A 15-day-pay discount is real in counties and uncertain at big state hospital systems.

## 5. Capital needs (A unless noted)

- **Operating:** At $100M of premium, a 15-45 day gap between paying hospitals and being reimbursed by the state ties up $4-11M of working capital. A TPA license and URAC accreditation are table stakes (Polk). Add a performance bond, which is typical of state contracts (U).
- **Loss capital:** to survive one 15-20% volume shock (Oregon's was 17%) I would want surplus or a reinsurance quote of 15-20% of premium, $15-20M. The gate figure of "$60-70M" applies to an insurer and is not what this idea needs.
- **Funding path:** a services business with low margin and a few large customers is a poor venture fit. It is closer to a Medicaid managed-care shop and would likely need a strategic backer.

## 6. Regulatory and liability

- **Licensing:** TPA licensing follows NAIC Model 90-1 in most states, and insurers and HMOs are often exempt from it (Delaware text). [Delaware](https://legis.delaware.gov/SessionLaws/Chapter?id=41967) (S) Eight states have vendors holding hospital risk under all-inclusive capitation (Pew), and none of the sources I read mention an insurer license, so a service-contract structure is plausible but unconfirmed. I found no state opinion on a stand-alone per-member off-site contract (gap).
- **Liability:** the idea's own advantage, utilization review that gets referrals done on time, makes the company the gatekeeper. Private medical contractors in prisons act under color of state law for civil-rights claims (West v. Atkins, background knowledge, not re-verified). Recent verdicts show denied-care exposure, for example a $763K Indiana verdict against Centurion for denied kidney treatment (PLN headline, U). Professional-liability capacity is tightening (Wellpath cited insurance issues).
- **Rates:** state statutes can cut the discount you sell and also cap what hospitals will take, so a Medicare-plus network can fail to form. Florida's DOC bill HB 913 would let DOC-contracted providers be paid above 110% of Medicare, which I read as a sign that contracted hospitals want a premium (A; bill status unconfirmed).

## 7. Is the why-now real?

Partly. The failure wave is real (Wellpath Chapter 11, YesCare, Illinois, Alabama, Kansas). But buyers answered with replacements, and the thin hospital-payment arrears show up as vendor risk, not as an appetite for a new structure. Medicaid expansion shrinks the manageable inpatient pool, and nine states have trigger laws to end expansion if the federal share falls below 90% (AZ, AR, IL, IN, MT, NH, NC, UT, VA). [KFF Health News](https://kffhealthnews.org/news/article/medicaid-expansion-funding-trigger-laws-9-states-trump-administration/) (S) Work requirements start in 2027 (U). I found nothing on how the 2025 federal budget law changed the inmate inpatient exception (gap).

## 8. The upside-case assumptions

| Assumption | Evidence | Read |

The operator eats downside when values fall and the lender sees windfall as its own.

- **Insurance and licensing.** Wrongful-repossession GL of $1M/$2M, on-hook $100K, garagekeepers $350K recommended; a forwarder cannot technically buy garagekeepers and uses a property-of-others policy [S] https://resolvion.com/managing-risk-understanding-insurance-coverages/. Illinois requires $1M/$3M for agencies [S] https://ilga.gov/legislation/ilcs/documents/022504220K90.htm.
- **Scale needs sponsor capital.** The two scaled forwarders have PE owners (Kinderhook; SBJ and TZP), and Primeritus's CARS deal alone was a $102.5M facility. A 50-agency pilot is cheap. A national operator is not [A].

## 8. Regulatory and liability

- **Breach of peace sits on the secured party.** An Illinois court awarded $24K+ against a repo company in Oct 2025 [S] https://www.accountsrecovery.net/2025/10/14/judge-awards-24k-after-repo-found-to-breach-the-peace/. A California court kept a bank in a wrongful-repossession case in Dec 2025 [S] https://www.accountsrecovery.net/2025/12/29/judge-denies-mtd-in-fdcpa-rfdcpa-case-over-repossession/. A Nevada footnote says secured parties answer for agents [S] https://swlaw.com/publication/nevada-court-of-appeals-clarifies-what-constitutes-a-breach-of-the-peace-when-repossessing-vehicles. An operator paid on net proceeds will be asked whether the incentive rewards aggressive grabs.
- **Licensing.** Michigan's Supreme Court held in June 2014 that forwarding is a collection activity [S] https://curepossession.com/michigan-supreme-court-rules-against-forwarders; Illinois exempts pure forwarders [S] https://lig.ilga.gov/legislation/ilcs/documents/022504220K30.htm; California is the strictest. The "scheduled hand-back" step means contacting borrowers, which likely brings state collection licensing and Reg F/TCPA exposure [A, counsel needed].
- **LPR (the locate input).** Easing: California's appeals court affirmed summary judgment for DRN on July 20, 2026, requiring actual harm [S] https://www.passwordprotectedlaw.com/2026/07/california-court-rules-automated-license-plate-recognition-law-requires-actual-harm/. Tightening: Arkansas's AG said in Dec 2023 that LPR for repossession is illegal [S] https://hudsoncook.com/article/arkansas-limits-use-of-license-plate-readers-for-repossession. Kentucky HB 58 (90-day retention, limits on commercial use, borrower disclosure from 2027) awaited the governor in April 2026; I did not confirm its outcome [S] https://curepossession.com/kentucky-bill-seriously-threatens-lpr-data-access-for-the-repossession-industry/. Colorado's repossession bill failed in 2026 [S] https://curepossession.com/colorado-lpr-bill-dies-but-a-trend-is-developing/.
- **Federal vacuum, political heat.** The CFPB rescinded its repossession bulletin in 2025 [S, search summary] https://niada.com/dashboard/?p=5928 and Senator Warren sent 12 letters in Feb 2026 [S] https://www.banking.senate.gov/newsroom/minority/with-trump-sidelining-cfpb-warren-launches-probe-into-the-auto-lending-industry-as-car-repossessions-skyrocket. Enforcement shifts to state AGs and private suits [S] https://www.goodwinlaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/03/insights-finance-cfs-yir-auto-loan-origination-and-servicing.

## 9. Why now: half real

Real: repossessions have sat at the highest level since 2009 for two years (Cox ~1.7M at auction, flat through 2029). Fitch subprime delinquency was 5.80% at mid-2026 vs 5.60% at mid-2025 (6.13% in July), and annualized subprime net loss 8.42% vs 8.17% [S] https://www.autoremarketing.com/?p=130785. Wholesale values are soft, and Cox's mid-September deck reportedly notes the Fed's first hike since 2023 (search summary; Cox link above). Used up: this is a plateau, not a shock. Subprime delinquency eased from 6.50% at year-end 2025 to 5.80% at mid-2026 (same Fitch source). The Tricolor-era investor-reporting demand is unsupported by anything I found.

## 10. Assumption ledger (the upside case, tested)

| Claim in idea / gate | What I found | Status |
|---|---|---|
| "Nobody is paid on net proceeds" | Percent-of-recovery (Servicing Solutions) and time-tiered fees (Chase) exist. Net-per-defaulted-dollar against a baseline was not found. | Partly refuted |
| "Locate-first is a gap; file assigned at day 60-90" | Day 60-90 confirmed at CPS, but Resolvion sells pre-charge-off skip at day 15-25 and LPR staging, and DRN sells day-30 contact lender-direct. | Refuted as a gap |
| "29% recovery means most assignments fail" | CFPB: includes cures, voluntary and redemptions; no split. | Refuted |
| "Voluntary hand-back costs a fraction" | $265 vs $365 agent pay. | Overstated |
| "$650 net per unit; 154k units = $100M" | Needs transport outside the bill. At $400 it is 250k units. | Fragile |
| "3-5 anchors at 15-25k repos consolidate onto one invoice" | Panel norm is 3-4 vendors with quarterly reallocation. Big lenders run in-house vendor teams. | Contradicted |
| "Pilot of 1,000 accounts proves +3 points" | Subprime recovery moved 1.5 points in one month. 1,000 accounts at 30-40% sale recovery is a noisy test. | Needs randomization and larger n |
| "Compliance holds" | State LPR bills, breach-of-peace suits, licensing for borrower contact. | Open |
| "DRN plate data is the locate source" | DRN owns forwarder brands and has cut forwarders before. | Dependency risk |

## 11. Verdict and what would change it

As specified, this is a forwarder with a better contract. The customers it can win cheaply (CUs) are too small, the customers that are big are served by incumbents and in-house teams, and the one differentiator (net-proceeds pricing) is a term sheet, not a moat. The only route to $100M I can see is **buying forwarders**: capital-heavy and thin-margin. The idea should not be narrowed into a CU boutique; that is the "shrink to survive" failure.

**Would raise my score:** a randomized pilot of 3,000+ accounts at one 20k+ lender showing 3+ points of net-dollar recovery at p<0.05, plus a written commitment of 30%+ of that lender's flow. Also a DRN-independent locate source.

## Gaps

- No 2025-26 forwarder rate card, revenue or market-share data (Primeritus and Resolvion revenue figures are aggregator estimates; incfact's $100M/$89M list is unreliable).
- No sourced lender count by repossession volume; Exeter and CPS repossession counts are my estimates.
- Days-to-sale and auction/transport/title fee figures are unverified (single low-quality source).
- DRN's pricing and whether it sells locate-only to lenders.
- Final status of Kentucky HB 58, and any 2026 RDN/Cox repossession totals.

For: owners outsource design under multi-year alliances (above); one major utility awarded GSE a $35M/2-year staff-augmentation master agreement in 2020 [S] ([Staffing Industry](https://www.staffingindustry.com/Editorial/Industrial-Staffing-Report/Dec.-17-2020/Contract-watch-GSE-Systems-awarded-two-master-services-agreements)); AtkinsRéalis-FANCO is up to CAD 250M (US$181M) over five years [S] ([NEI Mag](https://www.neimagazine.com/news/fanco-atkinsrealis-forge-alliance/)); PE paying a reported $1.25B of equity for Enercon.

Against or missing: I found no RFP, tender or owner statement asking for fixed-price AI-produced deliverables. MIT Technology Review's uprate story names price and equipment, not engineer shortage, as the constraint [V] ([MIT TR](http://www.technologyreview.com/2026/10/15/1146577/nuclear-power-upgrade)). Shortage data is workforce-level (IEA, USC), not overflow-demand-level.

## 5. Unit economics and capital

- **Rates.** One S&L 2022 invoice in a Texas filing shows $102-$270/hr from Associate I to Principal [S] ([PUC](https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/56211_218_1394038.PDF)). At about $160-200 blended and 1,500 billable hours, that is $240-300k per billable engineer. Actual all-in revenue per head: DP Engineering about $180k, Enercon about $120k [V/S]. So "400 engineers at $250k" understates staffing: about 450-560 total staff at today's productivity (rate model vs DP Engineering actuals; Enercon's ratio implies more) [I].
- **Margins.** DP Engineering's earn-out EBITDA thresholds ($2.75-4.3M on $20M+) imply 13-21% [V/I]; consulting firms generally run low-to-mid 20s% [S] ([Chaffe](https://www.bvresources.com/articles/bvwire/consulting-firm-multiples-climb-with-size-per-chaffe-analysis)).
- **AI lever [I].** Assume 30% fewer hours per deliverable and a 15% price cut: revenue per hour worked rises about 21% ($200 to $243). $100M then needs about 370-410 staff instead of 450-500 (rate model). That is a few EBITDA points, available to any rival using the same models, and independent verification (Criterion III) does not compress.
- **Capital.** DP Engineering sold in 2019 for $13.5M cash plus up to $5M earn-out (about 0.7x revenue upfront) [V]. 2026 pricing is higher: lower-middle-market engineering 4-8x EBITDA, specialists 9-12x [S] ([CT Acquisitions](https://ctacquisitions.com/?p=15590)); technical services index 12.5x in Q1 2026 [S] ([Investec](https://www.investec.com/advisory?p=58126)). Reaching $100M by acquisition at about 1.0-1.5x revenue is $60-120M plus working capital: PE-scale, not founder-scale [I]. Pilot plus a software-QA plan is low seven figures [I, unsourced].

## 6. Regulatory and liability landscape

- **Appendix B** [V] ([eCFR](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-10/chapter-I/part-50/appendix-Appendix%20B%20to%20Part%2050)): the licensee "shall retain responsibility" for the QA program (Criterion I); design checking must be by people other than the original designers (III); the licensee assesses supplier effectiveness at intervals (VII). A supplier cannot absorb the owner's accountability; it sells process comfort.
- **Part 21** [V] ([eCFR](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-10/chapter-I/part-21/section-21.3)): "basic component" includes safety-related design, analysis and consulting services, so suppliers carry defect-evaluation and reporting duties.

- **Approved-supplier path.** NUPIC audits need a supplier with at least five NRC-licensee customers; the standard cycle is 33 months [V] ([NUPIC](https://www.nupic.com)). I found no source for the idea's "12-24 months." A greenfield entrant is in a catch-22, which is why acquisition is the route. Rebuilding an acquired firm's QA program and tools may trigger customer re-acceptance [I]. NEI 22-04 Rev 1 (Aug 2026) would let ISO 9001 suppliers serve safety-related work because NQA-1 suppliers are shrinking [S] ([NRC](https://www.nrc.gov/docs/ML2621/ML26219A186.pdf)); helpful for scarcity now, erodes it if approved (aimed at components).
- **Professional licensure.** NSPE says reviewing documents after preparation, without involvement in design, does not meet "responsible charge" [S] ([NSPE](https://nspe.org/node/25565)). Where state PE seals apply, AI-drafts-human-reviews is legally weaker.
- **Insurance.** ISO generative-AI exclusion endorsements took effect Jan 1, 2026 and some carriers exclude AI claims from E&O [S] ([Jenner](https://www.jenner.com/en/news-insights/publications/in-law360-partner-david-kroeger-examines-emerging-ai-insurance-exclusions)); no policy text seen. A fixed-price, rework-guaranteed AI house may carry uninsured risk. Price-Anderson (to 2065) covers nuclear-incident claims, not contract or rework losses [S] ([Morgan Lewis](https://www.morganlewis.com/blogs/upandatom/2024/04/congress-gives-40-year-extension-for-price-anderson-nuclear-liability-framework)).

## 7. Is the why-now real?

Partly. Real: restarts, $4.3B of Constellation uprates, DOE loans, thin engineer pipeline (about 15,400 nuclear engineers nationally, median wage $135,760 [V]). Overstated: the drafting speedup is public (INL, DOE) and open to all; DOE's roadmap is closing the "unowned AI output" gap; incumbents are buying AI and capital. A first-mover window is 12-24 months at most [I].

## 8. Do the upside assumptions hold?

| Assumption | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| a. Buy an approved boutique in year 1 | DP Engineering comp; but Arlington, Pelican and New Mountain have add-on mandates | Plausible, price contested |
| b. AI removes 40%+ of hours on bounded deliverables | INL 2026 case study: experts estimated about 50% savings on a safety-document chapter, but found hallucinations, missing parameters and AI artifacts, on gpt-4o; "acceptable first draft" [V] ([INL](https://nric.inl.gov/content/uploads/34/2026/07/RPT-26-90824-Rev-0-Evaluation-of-AI-Enabled-Digital-Documented-Safety-Analysis-A-Case-Study.pdf)). DOE test is drafting-only with no error count. Westinghouse claims 25%. No data on calculations or design changes | Unproven; credible only for drafting-heavy work |
| c. 5+ owner QA groups accept software QA in 24 months | No precedent found; EPRI/INPO's NIVA pilot slides mark output "UNVERIFIED" [S] ([EPRI](https://restservice.epri.com/publicattachment/97144)) | Unproven |
| d. Hire about 250 engineers | Really about 370-560 staff; S&L alone grew 14.5% | Hard |
| e. Developer and restart licensing adds $25-35M | Developers award engineering to exclusive EPC alliances (AtkinsRéalis-FANCO; Hyundai-TerraPower [S] ([Neutron Bytes](https://neutronbytes.com/2026/08/14/terrapower-signs-hyundai-as-epc-for-eight-natrium-reactors/))); Everstar and EXCEL own the AI-licensing angle | Likely $10-20M as a subcontractor |
| f. Incumbents do not match for 3+ years | S&L AI hire, Westinghouse CMIS, Pelican portfolio, Enercon capital | Unlikely to hold |

## 9. Synthesis

Scenarios [I]: Bull 10% (requires b through f together; $100M+ by year 7). Base 40-45% (roll up two or three boutiques, a handful of owners, $25-45M). Bear 45-50% (stalls under $15M or is absorbed by Pelican/Enercon).

Durable advantage: approved-supplier listing plus accepted per-plant templates (moderate switching costs). Structural vulnerabilities: services margins; a commoditizing AI edge; owners keep the liability so will not pay a premium for "accountability"; E&O insurability. Current state is early and contested.

What would change my mind: one owner signing a multi-year fixed-price deliverable contract; NRC or EPRI language that independently verified AI output needs no separate tool QA; a qualified boutique available below 6x EBITDA.

Cheapest next test (2-3 months): interview 10 design-engineering directors on percent outsourced, appetite for per-deliverable pricing, and whether their QA group would require NQA-1 on the tool; run one paid calculation-revision pilot with the owner's engineer verifying; get E&O quotes with AI use disclosed; ask a broker for 2-3 boutique targets and valuations. Founder fit: this needs a credentialed nuclear QA and licensing insider plus institutional capital.

**Unverified:** outsourced-engineering pool; S&L and Enercon revenue; per-plant calculation and design-change volume; E&O policy text; NRC licensee AI guidance; Nuclearn's NRC deck and the Axios Atomic Canyon piece (403 on fetch; snippet only).

It calls the district court's use of Jackson v. Indiana 'probably inappropriate' and says substantive due process does not entitle plaintiffs to a 21-day limit. It says the waitlist 'is likely to pass [rational basis] with flying colors' and that 'HHSC must start redirecting its resources immediately' if there is no stay. The benchmarks, monitoring and four-year clock are all frozen. Without the order, the 'why now' disappears and Texas has no legal duty to buy a bed. The order is labeled preliminary and a merits panel will decide, but the first factor of the stay test is 'strong showing of likelihood of success,' so this is a bad sign for the plaintiffs. Texas also never needed the order to be a buyer: the pre-ruling waitlist was already down about 40% from its Dec 2022 peak with no new private operator involved.

THE MONEY IS GOING TO STATE-OWNED AND UNIVERSITY-OPERATED BEDS, WHICH ARE A PRICE-FREE SUBSTITUTE. HHSC's FY2028-29 request (submitted Sept 2026) protected state hospitals from the 3% cut. Coverage of the request mentions no forensic or contracted-bed ask and no cost estimate for meeting the order. The legislature has put more than $2.5B into state hospital builds since 2017, adding 680+ owned beds. Six more projects finish in 2027 (175 net new beds, 540 replaced or converted). The new 292-bed Dallas hospital is run by UT Southwestern, and the Houston, Lubbock and Amarillo hospitals are also university-linked builds. The statutes that fund contracted forensic capacity (SB 1677) name nonprofits and governmental entities, and Hays County's new jail-based program is a state grant to Hill Country MHMR, not to a private operator. A for-profit entrant is competing with the buyer's own balance sheet and with grant-funded public entities. The dossier's own number, $3.7M per state-built bed, shows the state is willing to pay far more to own capacity than a bed-day contract would cost.

THE INCUMBENTS ALREADY HOLD THE SHELLS AND THE TRACK RECORD, AND THE ASSET-LIGHT ROUTE LEAVES A NEW ENTRANT AS A JUNIOR PARTNER. Recovery Solutions (the ex-Wellpath behavioral unit, now lender-owned and debt-free) has about 3,700 staff in 70 facilities, and its website now says 12 states. It holds Florida's 446 privatized forensic beds. It won Washington's Maple Lane program through competitive procurement in 2015 and manages Montgomery County TX, where the CEO calls it the 'junior partner.' Liberty Healthcare holds the jail-based niche: Riverside County gave it a sole-source five-year contract (Jan 2024 to Dec 2028, about $2.9M a year) and San Bernardino was Liberty's earlier win. Texas requires a licensed hospital with Joint Commission accreditation for inpatient restoration, so the 'modular, 6-12 month' unit is not a sellable product. That leaves two options. Build and own at $0.5-3.7M per bed, which a startup cannot finance. Or manage someone else's shell at a thin fee, which is where Recovery Solutions already sits with a lender-owned balance sheet and no debt service. An incumbent response is trivial: it bids the same county-built shells with an existing licensed staff pool.

PRIVATE FORENSIC CAPACITY IS BOUGHT AS A TEMPORARY BRIDGE, AND BUYERS WRITE THE EXIT INTO THE CONTRACT. Washington's Trueblood settlement set a hard closure date of July 1, 2024 for the Maple Lane program, whether or not wait-time triggers were met. Closure is also tied to a median wait of 9 days or less for four consecutive months. Yakima's operator, Comprehensive Healthcare, quit mid-contract in 2021 over workforce shortages, so the operator-side failure mode is real. Colorado's April 2026 budget memo (as summarized in search results) shows 640 competency beds, of which only 84 are private contracts (about 13%) and 96 are jail-based. The decree ends 2027-12-01. Florida's DCF reportedly asked for no new forensic bed funding in its 2026-27 request despite its own gap analysis showing 2,000+ beds needed by 2029 (from a summary of a 2026 complaint, so not primary). The pattern is that states under litigation fund state builds first and rent private beds only as an interim, and the rental ends when the state's capacity opens. A five-year availability contract is exposed to this ramp-down, and 600 beds at one operator has no precedent in any of the four states.

NO ONE WANTS THIS ASSET, AND THE ECONOMICS DO NOT CLEAR EVEN IF BEDS ARE BOUGHT. Wellpath's whole behavioral unit ($425M revenue, about 3,000 patients, 20+ years) drew about 70 NDAs and no qualifying outside bid. The lenders took it for a $395M credit bid, about 0.93x revenue. Capital markets have already passed on the scaled version of this business twice. At the margins in the dossier (8-12% EBITDA, with a Texas private operator saying it loses money at a $529 rate against $700-900 cost), $100M of revenue is $8-12M of EBITDA with a hard-to-insure forensic patient cohort (the 2025 Florida wrongful-death suit is the tail risk). The cheaper jail-based and outpatient alternatives set the price anchor: Harris County at $261, Liberty San Bernardino at about $170 and Colorado jail-based at $421. The first SB 528 cost comparison in Aug 2027 gives HHSC a public benchmark to push private rates down. Texas jail-based programs restore poorly (10 of 19 restored half or fewer), so a high price needs a high-acuity inpatient product that only licensed hospitals can sell.

# C11 Dossier: P062 "Outreach Without Selling" (gate pick "Outreach Partner Labs")

Researched 2026-10-18. Method: about 50 searches and fetches, plus primary filings read directly (Quest 10-K FY2024, Labcorp 10-K FY2021, CMS manual chapter 16, 42 CFR 424.73, XiFin 2026 report, Quest Q4 2025 prepared remarks, Sonic FY26 deck). Tags: (S) sourced, (A) my arithmetic or assumption, (U) unverified. Pages that returned 403 (Business Wire, Sonic's site, GenomeWeb) were used only through search summaries and are marked "search summary".

## 1. Verdict

**Weak, trending dead as a $100M business. I would not advance it as written.**

- The pool is real and large.
- The $100M revenue figure is arithmetically reachable only as consolidated JV revenue. That revenue earns about $8-15M of EBITDA and needs roughly $120M+ of equity at the multiples national buyers actually pay (A).
- The plan fails four checks:
  - The legal structure contradicts Medicare billing rules.
  - Capital is understated by about 2x.
  - The competitor set is far bigger than "none found".
  - The closest funded precedent (RDL, $250M committed in 2012) had stalled by 2015 after backing away from deals.
- My estimate (A), 5-7 years out:

| Case | Probability | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Bear | ~50% | No controlled JV closes; 2-4 management contracts, $2-6M revenue, or a pivot to advisory |
| Base | ~35% | One JV plus a few managed systems; $35-45M revenue, $3-5M EBITDA |
| Bull | ~15% | 2-3 JVs plus 8 managed systems; $100-130M revenue, $10-15M EBITDA, $120M+ invested |

- Median is about $8-12M, below the gate's $20M. Upside is about $100M of revenue but not $100M of value creation.

## 2. Industry metrics (step 0)

Outreach runs on:
- net revenue per test or requisition
- contribution margin %
- cash collected per dollar billed
- volume growth
- sale price as a multiple of revenue

## 3. Market and bottom-up (steps 1-2)

**The pool**
- Quest's investor day sizes hospital outreach at about $20B of a $58B physician channel across "600+ health systems", with about 20 Quest deals in a decade. (S) [Quest 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1022079/000094787125000321/ss4596431_ex9901.htm)
- That is about $33M per system (A).
- Program sizes are skewed. Chi's 2016 survey had a median of $12.8M and a mean of $24.9M. Contribution margin was 23-33%, defined as revenue less dedicated and incremental outreach costs. (S) [CLP survey summary](https://clpmag.com/resource-center/research/survey-laboratory-outreach-enjoys-favorable-profitability/)
- Hospital labs were 13.6% of 6,411 PAMA reporters, about 870 NPIs. These are NPIs, not systems. (S, computed) [CMS fact sheet](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/preliminary-calendar-year-cy-2027-medicare-clinical-laboratory-fee-schedule-payment-rates)

**Flow of deals** (the real constraint)
- Quest and Labcorp closed at least 29 outreach deals from 2013 to 2024, all to the nationals, with prices undisclosed. (S) [G2 deal list](https://www.g2intelligence.com/dx-deals-outreach-deals-by-quest-labcorp-are-still-ramping-up/)
- Kaufman Hall counted about 2 transactions a year in 2013-2021 and 7 in 2022. (S) [HFMA](https://www.hfma.org/finance-and-business-strategy/healthcare-business-trends/strategic-alternatives-abound-for-health-system-outreach-laboratories/)
- Labcorp's CEO said it had 13 new or closed hospital or regional lab deals in 2025. (S, search summary) [360Dx](https://www.360dx.com/clinical-lab-management/labcorp-reaffirms-outreach-acquisitions-jpm-key-growth-cites-strong-deal)
- So roughly 5-13 systems a year decide to monetize (A). If 10-25% would pick a partner over cash (A, my assumption), 1-3 contestable systems appear a year.

**Two ways to $100M**

| Path | Math (A) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Fees | 9% of a $35M program is about $3.2M a system; $100M needs about 32 systems, about 5% of all systems | At 1-3 contestable a year, 10-30 years |
| Consolidated JV revenue | About 3 JVs at $33M | Needs the equity in section 6 |

- Verdict on the pool: size is not the problem. Velocity, capital and win rate against cash buyers are.

## 4. Competitors: gate claims tested (steps 4-8)

**Confirmed**
- Quest Co-Lab:
  - Revenue grew from about $300M (2019) to $800M (2024). (S) Same investor day deck.
  - The Corewell JV is 51/49, covering 21 hospitals, with a new lab due Q1 2027. (S) [press release](https://s2.q4cdn.com/390454341/files/doc_news/Corewell-Health-and-Quest-Diagnostics-Complete-Laboratory-Joint-Venture-Transaction-in-Michigan-2026.pdf)
  - Quest's own pitch: "Hospitals value our flexible solutions for accessing expertise, innovation and capital." (S) [Q4 2025 remarks](https://s2.q4cdn.com/390454341/files/doc_financials/2025/q4/Quest-Diagnostics-2025-Q4-Year-End-Webcast-Script.pdf) This is the startup's pitch, from a bigger and better-funded seller.
- Labcorp:
  - It bought CHS for $195M and has Parkview pending. (S) [Labcorp](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/press-releases/community-health-systems-announces-definitive-agreement-sell), [MedTech Dive](https://www.medtechdive.com/news/Labcorp-deal-Parkview-Health-outreach-lab-assets/805514/)
- Sonic USA:
  - It is flat on organic growth, and its operating review is ongoing. (S) [Sonic FY26](https://announcements.asx.com.au/asxpdf/20260820/pdf/072zhg5rhzbt79.pdf)
  - It has hospital JVs such as ProMedica, where over 90% of testing is done at the JV core lab. (S, search summary) [Sonic](https://www.sonichealthcareusa.com/about-us/news/promedica-health-system-in-new-joint-venture-partnership/)
- ARUP and Mayo are free or cheap advisory substitutes. ARUP offers an outreach-value assessment. (S) [ARUP](https://www.aruplab.com/magnify26/commercial-laboratories-want-buy-your-lab-operations-heres-why-math-not-your-favor)
- Consultants: Chi Solutions, owned by PE-created Accumen, which sells shared-savings partnerships. (S) [Dark Report](https://www.darkintelligencegroup.com/the-dark-report/laboratory-management/accumen-acquires-chi-to-beef-up-lab-consulting/)

**Refuted or changed**
- "No independent operator runs the commercial half."
  - **Orion Laboratories and FMOL Health.** In January 2026 they announced a JV in Louisiana. Orion is described as the state's largest independent lab and contributes operations, technology and logistics. FMOL had been using Labcorp. Terms are undisclosed. (S) [Healthcare Journal BR](https://www.healthcarejournalbr.com/node/3348), [Business Report](https://www.businessreport.com/business/orion-labs-fmol-health-partner-to-expand-services-across-the-state)
  - **TriCore.** It is hospital-owned and runs lab management for other systems, such as Lovelace. (S) [TriCore](https://www.tricore.org/lovelace-health-system-selects-tricore/)
  - **Atalan.** Froedtert's WDL launched this with HealthEco in 2023 as a hospital-lab network. I found no member list or update. (S) [MLO](https://www.mlo-online.com/management/article/53074544/froedtert-health-wisconsin-diagnostic-laboratories-and-healtheco-launch-atalan)
  - **Mednet Services.** It was an older "direct and network-based outreach" operator partnered with ARUP. Current status unknown. (S) [BioSpace](https://www.biospace.com/arup-laboratories-signs-agreement-with-b-mednet-services-b-to-expand-its-outreach-services)
- PAML as the "independent operator":
  - It was owned by Providence and CHI, with about $300M of revenue and 1,600 staff when sold to Labcorp. (S) [Lund Report](https://www.thelundreport.org/content/paml-announces-sale-labcorp), [Labcorp](https://www.labcorp.com/labcorp-acquire-pathology-associates-medical-laboratories-providence-health-services-and-catholic)
  - Its end state was a sale by its hospital owners, not an independent success.

**In-house substitutes**
- Tucson Medical Center took outreach back after selling it in 2003. Bryan Health built its own program. (S) [ARUP](https://www.aruplab.com/magnify26/commercial-laboratories-want-buy-your-lab-operations-heres-why-math-not-your-favor)
- Kootenai Health had a PAML JV with a 50/50 revenue split. PAML ran preanalytics and billing while Kootenai tested. Labcorp bought PAML in 2017 and converted it into a testing agreement with a 5-year noncompete. Kootenai says it was "losing money", insourced in 2022 with Mayo Outreach Insights, and reports EBIDA up about $10M from FY2022 to FY2024. (S) [CAP Today](https://www.captodayonline.com/how-a-core-lab-took-back-its-outpatient-business/)
  - This is the best published case of this exact model. The operator took half the revenue, the sponsor was acquired and changed the terms, and the hospital left.

**Software:** MEDITECH outreach portal, hc1 and similar tools are commodity enablers, not competitors. (U)

## 5. Evidence of demand and willingness to pay

**Positive**
- Hospitals do pay for outside lab operations: Quest's Co-Lab grew about 22% a year.
- The JV template is accepted: Corewell, FMOL/Orion, ProMedica.
- Distress is real:
  - Median health-system margin was -0.6% in January 2026 (Strata via ARUP). (S)
  - 43.5% of 2025 healthcare M&A involved a distressed party. (S)
  - Labcorp's CEO says Medicaid cuts and the end of ACA subsidies may push systems to sell. (S, search summary)
- Outreach billing is bad:
  - For hospital outreach, "procedure not paid separately" was 61.2% of denials and duplicates 22.6%.
  - Appeals recover 0.03% of receipts at $48 each. (S) [XiFin 2026](https://media.xifin.com/prod/uploads/EWC-2026-XiFin-2026-Payor-Denial-Impact-Report.pdf)

**Negative**
- Every one of the 29+ listed outreach exits went to Quest or Labcorp. I found no US case of a system choosing a venture-backed operator over cash.
- I found no open RFP for an outreach operating partner (search limited to public web).
- Sellers skew distressed, and distressed sellers want cash, not a 49% stake:
  - Jefferson sold its lab business for $108M against $231M of operating loss (FY2023).
  - Tufts cut about 600 jobs after its sale.
  - CHS was pruning non-core assets. (S) [Becker's](https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/finance/jefferson-sells-lab-business-for-108m/), [Digital Health News](https://www.digitalhealthnews.com/chs-completes-194m-sale-of-outpatient-lab-assets-to-labcorp)
- The signer is the CFO. Budget exists in the sense that outreach P&L exists, but the alternative on the table is a check.

## 6. Unit economics and capital

**National analogs**

| Item | Figure |
|---|---|
| Quest 2025 adjusted operating margin | 15.9% (S) [8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1022079/000102207926000005/dgx123120258-kexhibit991.htm) |
| Quest Corewell Co-Lab | About $250M of 2026 revenue "at low single-digit margins" (S, Q4 2025 remarks) |
| Labcorp on outreach acquisitions | Margins "typically lower than the company average early on" (S) [MedTech Dive](https://www.medtechdive.com/news/labcorp-buys-baystate-health-outreach-lab/695687/) |

- A scaled, synergy-rich national earns 16%. Management-type revenue earns a few points. A startup does not beat that.

**Prices paid**
- Ascension: $400M for assets with about $150M of annual revenue, or 2.7x. (S) [Labcorp release](https://labcorp.com/labcorp-announces-2021-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-results), [10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/920148/000092014822000015/lh-20211231.htm)
- The gate cites BioReference at 2.4x (not re-verified by me).
- Quest's 2024 outreach buys were $230M, $200M and $183M. Revenue was undisclosed. (S) [Quest 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1022079/000102207925000044/dgx-20241231.htm)
- Conflict to note: MedTech Dive says Quest paid "$2.2B" for outreach. The 10-K says $2.2B is the aggregate for all 2024 deals, including LifeLabs at about US$1B. The three outreach buys total $613M.

**Capital (A)**
- At 2.4-2.7x, a 51% stake in $100M of outreach revenue costs about $122-138M. The gate assumed $50-90M at 1.0-1.3x.
- Nationals can pay that because they cut costs by moving testing into their own hubs. Labcorp expected to "return its cost of capital by year two" on Ascension.
- A standalone operator cannot. At an 8-15% margin, $100M of revenue is worth $80-180M at 10-12x EBITDA (A), against $122-138M paid for 51% of it.
- RDL's CEO said the same thing in 2015: hospital lab payment levels differed from independent-lab levels, prices exceeded likely value, and RDL backed away from deals. (S) [G2](https://g2intelligence.com/?p=1172)

**Hospital's side of the fee (A)**
- A $33M program at 25% contribution is $8.3M.
- A 9% fee is $3.0M, or 36% of that contribution.
- The hospital's savings pool is 10-20% of addressable costs on vendor claims (Quest/Kaufman Hall). On about $25M of direct cost that is $2.5-5.0M. The fee consumes 60-120% of it.
- Selling at 2.7x pays about 10.7 years of contribution up front.
- Cost benchmarks for couriers, patient service centers and sales as a percent of revenue were not found, so the claim that 9% covers all commercial functions is unverified.

## 7. Legal and liability

1. **Medicare referral billing contradicts the structure.**
   - CMS manual ch. 16 §40.1 lets a referring lab bill for tests another lab performed only if:
     - it is in a rural hospital, or
     - the two are wholly owned by one another or by a third entity, or
     - it refers no more than 30% of its tests. (S) [CMS manual](https://www.cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Guidance/Manuals/Downloads/clm104c16.pdf)
   - A 51/49 LLC that bills while the hospital core lab does 80-85% of testing meets none of these, unless the hospital is rural.
   - I found no disclosed structure where an LLC bills for tests done in the hospital's lab. The JVs I found build or use a JV-owned performing lab (Corewell's new lab, with billing mechanics in the interim undisclosed; ProMedica's JV core lab). Kootenai instead billed Labcorp as the reference lab, and Labcorp performs most of its own testing.
   - The fix pushes capital and equipment into the JV, or reduces the model to a management contract.
2. **Billing-agent pay.**
   - Medicare may pay an agent only if the agent's compensation "is not related in any way to the dollar amounts billed or collected". (S) [42 CFR 424.73](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/42/424.73)
   - That blocks a percent-of-collections fee where the operator receives payment. Paying into a provider-controlled account may avoid it (U).
3. **EKRA.**
   - Payments to third-party marketers are covered. Percent pay is not per se unlawful, but it falls outside the safe harbor. (S) [Frier Levitt](https://www.frierlevitt.com/articles/ninth-circuit-clarifies-permissible-marketing-compensation-under-ekra-laboratories-beware/)
   - An operator with sales staff paid by percent of revenue is the target profile. This binds only the Ninth Circuit.
4. **Payer enrollment cuts both ways.**
   - Anthem New Hampshire has excluded most hospital labs since 2010. Frisbie opened an independent lab company to get back in. (S) [Dark Report](https://www.darkintelligencegroup.com/the-dark-report/clinical-laboratory-trends/locked-out-of-payer-network-nh-hospital-opens-lab-company/)
   - UnitedHealthcare's July 2026 Preferred Lab Network lists Eurofins, Labcorp, Quest and specialty labs, with no hospital lab. (S) [UHC](https://www.uhcprovider.com/en/resource-library/news/2026/preferred-lab-providers-july.html)
   - Re-enrolling at independent-lab rates opens networks but removes the premium. Hospital outpatient departments are paid about 3x independent labs, with 60% of spend. (S) [HCCI](https://healthcostinstitute.org/all-hcci-reports/price-markups-for-clinical-labs-employer-based-insurance-pays-hospital-outpatient-departments-3x-more-than-physician-offices-and-independent-labs-for-identical-tests/) Chi found nationals' net revenue per test about 20% below typical outreach.
5. **Gaps:** tax-exempt JV control rules (UBIT, Rev. Rul. 98-15), state laws and whether commercial payers copy the Medicare referral rule were not researched. Counsel is required.

## 8. Why-now
